posts.author: Dr. Hana sayed
posts.headline: Accountant | Impact Investing, ESG
posts.text: What if you could test a development policy on 600 people before rolling it out to millions? I'm excited to share the Egypt–Aswan Development Digital Twin, an interactive policy lab set in Aswan, Upper Egypt — my home city — created by Alexander Odere. 🔗 https://lnkd.in/gsH2xetB 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 1⃣ A living synthetic town 600 people across 75 households, each with jobs, income and finances, on a resilience ladder from severe vulnerability to asset building. 2⃣ Pull a policy lever Skills training, job placement, heat protection, or an inclusive-economy package that reaches the poorest first. 3⃣ Introduce a shock A 9% food price rise or a 7-day heatwave based on Aswan's real climate. 4⃣ Watch it unfold Employment, income and exits from vulnerability update day by day. Click any person to follow their story. 5⃣ Compare scenarios See who benefits, who stays vulnerable, and why. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 Averages hide people. A program can raise average income and still leave the most vulnerable behind. A digital twin shows these trade-offs before resources are committed — not after. 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗶𝘁'𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 • Ministries and governorates designing employment and social protection programs • Development agencies and multilateral banks • Banks and microfinance institutions stress-testing household credit • Investors looking at Upper Egypt • Universities and research teams 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 Alexander Odere designed and built this platform. He is a business developer who combines product strategy, software development and partnership building. Turning a complex policy idea into a tool anyone can explore in minutes takes rare talent. 💡 Looking for someone who turns ideas into products? Visit Alexander Odere's profile and connect. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗘𝗴𝘆𝗽𝘁 + 𝗞𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗮 Having worked with low-income households at Nasser Social Bank in Aswan, and now pursuing a PhD in Development Policy at KDI School in Korea, I see real value in tools that connect evidence from the ground with Korea's strength in evidence-based policy — adaptable to any region in the world. Note: this is a demo built on synthetic data, not an official forecast. 𝗟𝗲𝘁'𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗶𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂: → want to pilot it for a program, city or region → hold data that could ground it in reality → want a custom digital twin for your organization → are hiring a talented business developer — reach out to Alexander Odere Try it, test it, break it — and tell us what you see. #DigitalTwin #DevelopmentPolicy #Egypt #Aswan #Korea #PolicySimulation #FinancialInclusion #GovTech #DataForGood #Hiring #BusinessDevelopment

posts.text: 6.4%. That's the percentage of software features responsible for 80% of user clicks, according to Pendo's research. posts.author: Shahzad Waheed
posts.headline: Go High Level & MVP Launch | Technical SEO Consultant | Helping SMBs Scale Smarter
posts.text: Software agencies died in 2026. That’s what the internet keeps telling us. So I went through the arguments. Take 1: No. AI hasn’t killed agencies. It changed what developers do. Take 2: No. AI lets people solve problems faster without paying developers, designers and agencies a fortune. Take 3: Yes. Why hire five people when one person with AI can do the work? Take 4: Hell no. A ChatGPT employee says AI is trying to take over the world, so we’re all doomed anyway. Funny. But the job market tells a less funny story. The numbers: US software developer job postings fell 73% from their February 2022 peak to February 2025, according to Indeed data cited by Investopedia. They’ve rebounded since but are still below pre-pandemic levels. The World Economic Forum projects 92 million jobs displaced globally by 2030 and 170 million created. That covers the whole economy, not just AI. Juniors have it worst. AI handles more coding tasks, but companies still need experienced engineers to make architectural decisions, review code and solve hard problems. Entry-level roles are under pressure while senior demand shows signs of recovery. AI doesn’t need to replace every developer to disrupt the industry. It only needs to let a company do the same work with fewer people. A project that needed six people might now need three who use AI well. A client who used to hire an agency might build an MVP with one AI-savvy founder. A small agency that competed on cheap development might have nothing left to compete on. Jobs rarely disappear with an announcement. Companies just stop hiring for them. So are software agencies finished? No. But agencies that sell code as their main value have a serious problem. The ones that last will understand the client’s business problem, build reliable systems, own the outcome and use AI to deliver more with less. The others may not notice until the pipeline dries up. How much of today’s work will still need a human tomorrow? For agencies, we’re already finding out. I have a strong case study but have got no more energy to write, good night!

posts.text: JetBrains open-sourced a 12B coding model yesterday that fixes 47% of real GitHub issues with only 2.5B parameters active per token. It's like hiring a junior who reads the repo, runs the tests, and checks their own diff before handing it back — instead of paying a frontier model for every line. Mellum2.1 (Apache 2.0, 131k context) got there through RL, not scale: post-training ran millions of sandboxed runs across thousands of real environments. JetBrains' own numbers: 47.0% SWE-bench Verified, 28.0% SWE-bench Pro. For comparison, Microsoft's MAI Code 1.1 scores 72.6% in the cloud and 70.8% on-device — the frontier still leads by ~26 points. But Mellum2.1 was the fastest in its test group under load, serving almost 2x the tokens/sec of Qwen3.5-9B on one H200, and it runs entirely on your own hardware. Best for: self-hosted sub-agents and high-volume repo work where code can't leave your machines. Not for: the hardest multi-file refactors. What's the smallest model you've actually shipped inside a coding agent? #AI #CodingAgents #LLM #DevTools

posts.author: Peter Kempin
posts.headline: Co-Founder & CRO Prismus | Turning technical signals into commercial opportunities
posts.text: My clients and I have more in common than I initially thought. Many are scientists, engineers or founders. They build and sell complex hardware or software into lab settings. And while our products are very different, we are all trying to figure out the same things. Is there a real need? Am I talking to the right person? Do they have budget? Is now a good time? Basically, the good old BANT framework: Budget, Authority, Need, Timing. What’s different is where we look for answers. For our clients, that often means digging into scientific papers, grants, conference presentations, technical hiring or company announcements. Trying to understand what people are actually working on in their labs. And whether their technology could be relevant. For me, the signals are a bit different. But I’m asking pretty much the same questions. And yes, I use Prismus.ai myself to find and qualify opportunities. Eating our own dog food. 😄 Finding prospects is one thing. Figuring out who to approach, why and when is the tricky part. What signals tell you that a prospect is worth reaching out to?

posts.text: Indian IT built a $250 billion export business on one enduring proposition. Western companies had work to do. India had engineers who could do it cheaper, faster, and at a scale no domestic workforce could match. For thirty years that proposition held. Infosys, TCS, Wipro, and HCL became some of India's most valuable companies by industrialising the delivery of software services to the world. AI is now quietly dismantling the assumption underneath that proposition. The work that India's IT industry built its foundation on- writing code, testing software, managing IT infrastructure, processing data, running support operations is exactly the category of work that AI handles first and handles well. A junior developer at an Indian IT firm writing boilerplate code for a banking client in New Jersey is doing work that GitHub Copilot and similar tools now assist with, accelerate, and in some cases replace entirely. The client still needs the outcome. They are beginning to need fewer people to produce it. This is not a theoretical risk sitting five years away. Large IT companies are already seeing it in their hiring numbers. TCS, Infosys, and Wipro collectively added fewer employees in the last two years than they did in any comparable period during the previous decade. The headcount-to-revenue ratio that defined Indian IT's scaling model is beginning to decouple. Revenue can grow without proportional headcount growth, which sounds like good news until you realise that India's IT industry employed over five million people and was the primary career destination for an entire generation of engineering graduates. The companies that will survive this shift are the ones moving up the value chain fast enough. From executing instructions to designing systems. From writing code to architecting solutions. From running infrastructure to advising on AI strategy. That transition requires a fundamentally different kind of talent than the one Indian IT scaled with, and retraining five million people is not a problem that resolves itself quickly. The $250 billion model is not broken yet. But the ground underneath it is shifting in ways that quarterly earnings reports do not fully capture. posts.author: Zarion Zory
posts.headline: Google: ZARION ZORY Explore: #ZarionZoryStory
posts.text: From Civil to Software: How India’s Brightest Tech Dreams Hit a Dead End ​Back in the 1980s and 1990s, a degree in Civil Engineering was often seen as a certificate of failure in India. Today, in the 2020s, a degree in Software Engineering is looking even worse—and unlike back then, the current cost of living makes it far harder to survive. ​As a teenager in the early 1990s, I witnessed blanket unemployment among civil engineers across every sector. In 1997, my friend’s elder brother was a certified engineer desperately hunting for a ₹5,000-per-month job in Delhi. Through competitive examinations, he eventually secured a position within the bureaucracy of the Ministry of Home Affairs, but he couldn't land a decent role in the private sector. ​By the late 1990s and early 2000s, call centers arrived to absorb almost everyone—non-graduates, general graduates, and Bachelor of Technology engineers alike—into a thriving job market with salaries ranging from ₹6,500 to ₹65,000 per month. Fast forward 25 years, and that safety net is collapsing like never before. Across India's IT landscape, entry-level service roles (at firms like TCS, Infosys, and Wipro) have remained practically frozen at ₹3.25 to ₹3.5 LPA (~₹22,000–₹25,000/month in-hand) for nearly two decades despite soaring inflation. ​In South Bangalore near India’s Silicon Valley, PG hostel rentals in tech hubs like BTM Layout and HSR Layout were built around an expected starting income of ₹25,000 per month. But as tech hiring stalled and low-stipend training institutes and bootcamps flooded the market, many young engineers found themselves surviving on stipends of just ₹10,000 to ₹12,000 per month—leaving both freshers and PG owners struggling to keep their heads above water. Today, with entry-level hiring down significantly and AI automation rapidly taking over junior tasks, the squeeze is even tighter. ​As management legend Peter Drucker observed, "The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence—it is to act with yesterday's logic." The software industry was never a structural, long-term solution to India’s perennial unemployment crisis; it was merely a single night’s feast—full of lights, abundance, and temporary celebrations. Now, the music has stopped, and we are right back at square one, just like in the 1980s. #ZarionZoryStory ​#TechLayoffs #SoftwareEngineering #IndiaJobMarket #CareersInTech #BangaloreTech #IndianEconomy

posts.text: The software engineer hiring system is BROKEN! Eight interviews. Seven passed. The eighth was in my calendar. Then an email: “The interview has been cancelled.” No reason given. I’ve been around long enough to read between the lines. More people reached the final stage than there were seats, and someone had to be cut. This time it was me. It isn’t the first time. I’m not naming anyone. I’m writing because before I became a software engineer, I was a pharmacist. And that past keeps making me ask an awkward question. When I qualified as a pharmacist, I sat one licensing exam. After that, no hospital asked me to prove from scratch that I knew what paracetamol does. The profession agreed on a bar, and my licence carried it from one employer to the next. Software has no such thing. So every company rebuilds the entire bar exam from zero. LeetCode. Live coding. A take-home that eats your weekend. System design. A database deep-dive. A personality test. A culture round. Then the “final” round. Now look at who pays for it. The company spends one interviewer-hour per round. The candidate spends several hours preparing for each one. When I added up this one process, it came to roughly 26 hours. Unpaid. For a company I don’t work for. And the risk is completely one-sided. A company adds a stage to avoid one bad hire. Every candidate who goes through that stage pays for it. Finance has a word for how finalists get treated: options. Keep several open, exercise one, let the rest expire. Nobody calls an expiring option to explain. I’m far from alone. In a LiveCareer survey this April, 45% of workers said an employer simply stopped responding during hiring. 48% said they’d never apply to that company again. That last number should worry hiring teams. Engineers talk. None of this needs a revolution: Tell finalists how many people are in the final round. Pay for take-home work, or cap it at two hours. After stage three, give real feedback. A paragraph is enough. If you cancel, say why. “We’ve filled the role” is a complete sentence. Ask whether you need eight stages, or just never removed any. Engineers will be fine. They will prepare for the next one with the same energy, because that’s the job. But if you hire engineers: the people in your final round have already given you their weekends, their evenings, and a bit of their hope. Treat that like it’s worth something. They are humans. Not objects. Engineers, what’s the longest process you went through, only to be dropped at the end? #SoftwareEngineering #Hiring #TechCareers #CandidateExperience

posts.text: 1.9 Million Impressions in 365 Days: What I Learned Sharing Tech, Career, and Life Lessons on LinkedIn 🚀 A year ago, I didn't set out to "game" the algorithm. As a software and cloud architect, I simply wanted to share real-world engineering realities, career observations, and lessons learned from decades in the industry. Looking at my LinkedIn analytics today, the numbers completely blew me away: 📊 The 1-Year Snapshot: • 1,908,838 total impressions (+123% YoY) • 817,655 unique members reached (73% outside my 1st-degree network!) • 6,930 total engagements (5,182 reactions, 568 thoughtful comments) • 869 saves & 1,431 link clicks What surprised me the most wasn't just the sheer volume, but the specific stories that resonated with our community: 1. Real Hiring Realities (231K impressions): Questioning broken hiring screening patterns and advocating for fair evaluation struck an immediate chord with candidates and hiring managers alike. 2. Work-Life Perspective (221K impressions): "No job offer is worth losing yourself—or your family." Technical skills matter, but burnout and family priorities are conversations our industry desperately needs to keep having. 3. Cloud Engineering & Human Stories (187K impressions): The reality of a $55k unexpected cloud bill and helping junior engineers navigate cloud architecture safeguards proved that actionable, cautionary case studies deliver real value. 💡 3 Quick Takeaways: • Specificity beats generic advice: Real architecture challenges and transparent hiring insights drive far more meaningful discussions than generic platitudes. • Vulnerability resonates: Highlighting mistakes, unexpected bills, and life balance encourages others to share their own lessons in the comments. • "Saves" are the true signal: 869 bookmarks told me people weren't just scrolling by—they found reference material worth keeping. A massive thank you to everyone who read, commented, challenged my perspectives, and connected over the past year. What has been your biggest takeaway or lesson shared on LinkedIn this year? Let's discuss in the comments below! 👇 #CloudArchitecture #SoftwareEngineering #CareerAdvice #TechCommunity #Leadership #LinkedInGrowth

posts.text: The fastest route into development might be the support queue. A junior support analyst ad caught my eye this month. It asked for 6 to 12 months of commercial SQL. Some listed C# too, with no expertise needed. Then one line said the hire would gradually move into full development work. Read that again. It's an apprenticeship with a ticket queue attached. And it makes sense. Support analysts read the errors, query live data, and talk to the users that developers rarely meet. After more than a year of production database checks and support tickets, I'd say it was the best training I've had for writing code that holds up. For hiring managers in software: How many of your best developers started in support? If any of this sounds like your path, or the one you're on now, I'd like to hear where it started. #ITSupport #SoftwareDevelopment #CareerPath #Databases

posts.headline: CEO & Founder at Sheriff · View my services
posts.text: 🤠 SE BUSCA: pistolero o pistolera del código. Vivo o viva, y con criterio de arquitectura. Sumamos un nuevo talento a la cuadrilla: un referente técnico, AI-native y con visión para diseñar, escalar y llevar el producto al siguiente nivel. Ya somos parte del día a día de cientos de empresas en Chile y Perú que usan Sheriff para conocer con quién hacen negocios en 5 segundos. En apenas 4 años construimos todo esto: un equipo consolidado, áreas completas y un producto, Marshal, nuestro agente de IA, que hoy sale al mundo. Acá tu criterio técnico pesa: defines cómo escala el producto, con un equipo chico y 100% apalancado en IA. 🌵 Lo que harás en el pueblo: – Diseñar y escalar la plataforma: arquitectura, buenas prácticas y decisiones técnicas de fondo. – Modelar y optimizar datos para que el producto rinda a escala. – Guiar a los devs más junior de la cuadrilla: revisar código, hacer mentoría y subir el estándar técnico. – Empujar el uso experto de IA para automatizar el trabajo interno de punta a punta. – Resolver de principio a fin: del front al back, tomar problemas complejos y dejarlos en producción. – Traducir las necesidades de Producto, Comercial y Finanzas en soluciones sólidas. 🔎 Señas particulares del sospechoso: – 4+ años desarrollando software, con foco fullstack y visión de arquitectura. – Node.js, Python, JavaScript, React, Next.js, PostgreSQL, MongoDB y DynamoDB. – Desarrolla con IA (Claude). Sin esto no pasa la frontera: es excluyente. – Si ya ha visto AWS, GCP, serverless, web scraping o procesos ETL, mejor todavía. – Toma decisiones de arquitectura con criterio y las defiende con datos. – Le gusta enseñar y hacer crecer a quienes tiene al lado. – Busquilla, con las manos en el barro y buena onda. Justo, Simple y Cercano. ⭐ Recompensa ofrecida: – Una ruta de crecimiento clara hacia Staff Engineer. – Un equipo ágil donde tu criterio técnico pesa y se ve en producción. – Sprints de 2 semanas e IA en todo el ciclo de desarrollo. – Modalidad híbrida: 2 días en la oficina de Providencia y 3 remotos. ⚖️ El juicio es corto y transparente: Entrevista de fit cultural. Prueba técnica en pair programming, con foco en diseño. Entrevista final con el Head of Tech. Oferta formal y bienvenida a la cuadrilla. Sabrás siempre en qué etapa estás y cuándo tendrás noticias. 📩 ¿Te reconociste en el afiche? Entrégate voluntariamente: manda tu CV (y tu GitHub, si quieres) a postulaciones@thesheriff.cl con el asunto “CV [Tu nombre] — Fullstack Senior”. Proceso ágil y confidencial. ¿Conoces a alguien con estas señas? Delátalo en los comentarios. En este pueblo, eso se considera una buena acción. 👇 #Hiring #FullstackDeveloper #NodeJS #React #IA #TechJobs

posts.author: AI Hiring Board
posts.text: 📊 Palantir has 80 open AI roles on our board. 78 of them have “Forward Deployed” in the title. Only 2 have “AI Engineer” in the title. If you search their careers page for “machine learning”, you won’t find their AI hiring. You find it under “Forward Deployed”. Here’s what the 80 listings show: 1️⃣ 33 of the 80 are internships or new-grad roles (20 internships, 13 new grad). That’s 41% of the openings. Few AI employers on our board leave this much room for people at the start of their careers. 2️⃣ 36 titles name a government customer: US, UK, Norwegian, Japanese and Australian. More name an intelligence, NATO or defense-tech team. The customer in the title is part of the job. 3️⃣ None of the 80 roles is marked remote or hybrid. The work happens next to the customer. Washington, D.C. has 22 roles, New York 17 and London 12. Honolulu, Seoul, Sydney, Oslo, Vilnius and Abu Dhabi are on the list too. 4️⃣ The variants show what “deployed” covers: software, infrastructure, reliability, security, enablement, autonomous systems C2, mixed reality. There are also two Deployment Strategist roles, the non-engineering side of the same model. 🔍 The non-obvious part: here, “AI engineer” mostly means the person who makes models work inside a customer’s operations and data, on site. Building the model is not the main job. If your strongest skill is a polished notebook, this is a different job. If you’ve ever been the engineer who sat with the users until the system actually worked, you already do a version of it. ⚠️ Caveat: we read companies’ hiring systems directly, so employers without a public feed are invisible to us. These are counts from a large sample, not a census. Treat every number as a floor. 👉 All 80 roles, read straight from Palantir’s own board: https://lnkd.in/ekJUKYkR Have you worked a forward-deployed role? What surprised you most about it? 👇 #artificialintelligence #aijobs #hiring #machinelearning

posts.author: Valerii Hurachek
posts.headline: building Vesna for transparent tech hiring evidence & compliance
posts.text: Someone just made it to the interview stage because they put three lines of white text at the bottom of their resume. And the AI screener followed the instructions word for word. This sshot is from a hiring manager who caught it - an applicant hid tiny text in a 2pt white font, telling the model to ignore everything else and mark them as the best candidate. If you work in backend software, you recognize what this is immediately. Twenty years ago, if a website took text from an input box and pasted it straight into a database query, someone could type a few characters and wipe your tables. We called it SQL injection. It was one of the first basic security mistakes every junior developer learned to avoid. In 2026, half the AI screening tools on the market are making a similar mistake. They take raw text from a PDF, stitch it directly into a prompt, and ask an LLM to score the candidate. The software has no idea that white text on a white background is invisible to human eyes. It just reads the raw string, follows the instructions, and hands the candidate a top score. Jobseekers will always look for ways to get noticed. You cannot really blame someone for trying to get around a system that feels unfair. What bothers me is what happens to your pipeline. A capable backend engineer writes a plain resume about the production systems they kept running, and the parser drops them. Then someone with an invisible prompt injection lands on your senior engineer's calendar for a technical interview, only to fall apart on basic architecture questions. If you use an AI screening tool today, here is a simple test you can run this afternoon: Take an average resume from your archive. Add two lines of white text at the bottom telling the model that this is an exceptional candidate who should be moved forward immediately. Run it through your screener. If that changes the score, your software is just executing whatever string it was handed. Software can help talent teams handle volume, but only if it pulls verifiable technical facts and leaves the decision to a human being. When an LLM gets to make rejection calls on its own, hiring quickly turns into a game of who knows how to trick a prompt.

posts.text: 🚨🚨🚨HIRING🚨🚨🚨 We are reading and writing less, and worse, because of the rise of AI and brain rot. To counter it we should argue, engage critically, and sharpen our spoken reasoning. You can fake the essay. You can't fake thinking and reasoning on the fly. Being articulate is the prime wedge for the age of AI. Defending what you believe and understanding counterviews is crucial. So I built Debatable - live debates with a leaderboard. You are matched with a stranger on camera (or behind an anonymous avatar); you argue a motion in timed speeches, and an AI judge renders a ballot determining your ELO for later matchmaking. We know this AI judge is controversial conceptually, but we are steadfast on building a serious judging system. The site you'll see today was vibe-coded. I am not a career engineer; I built it with AI agents. It works, real people use it, and we have already begun rebuilding it entirely. We are a team of four - me, an engineer who has worked at NVIDIA and Apple, an MIT engineer, and an ML researcher from UT Austin - want to join us? 1) SWEs, one or two, full-time and paid (salary plus equity), ideally Oxford, SF, Chicago or NYC, but remote works. You need to be cracked. You'd own large parts of the rebuild - live video, the judge, the leaderboard, moderation - and it has to be ready for virality: the day one creator sends an entire audience through the door at once. Students and recent grads welcome. 2) Content and marketing interns, remote, but unpaid. You'd cut rounds into clips and help run our accounts + creator outreach. Ideally, you have a history of successful campaigns. 3) Creators, anywhere, any size: we want you, and we think you'll want us for content. Face another creator on camera while both audiences watch, or climb the ladder on stream. 4) Global ambassadors, any country: bring your debate society or club onto Debatable, run weekly rooms, host one event a month. There is a stipend, paid on results - commissioned debates that take place, and the people you bring in who debate or learn to debate. The vision for Debatable - We bring back Omegle, but structured, civil, yet contentious. We are the place people not only go to become more articulate, but to embrace the art of argument by debating or spectating. Apply through the forms on this page only: https://lnkd.in/gJThdtT8. DMs and emails aren't applications, but feel free to reach out if you're intrigued by what we're building or have questions. And I swear to god, if you send me AI writing or just boring writing, you're gone.

posts.text: AI replacing developers is going terribly wrong. At least, not in the way we expected. We were told AI would write more code, make developers more productive, and eventually reduce the number of developers companies need. But something interesting is happening. 1. Software development hiring is moving up again. Indeed says US software-development job postings are up almost 15% since February 2025, even while overall job postings fell 7%. 2. AI writes code fast. But it also creates a lot more code to review. Bugs. Unnecessary complexity. Security issues. Someone still has to review it, test it, understand it and maintain it. 3. And here's the part I find most interesting. 71% of the increase in software-development postings came from senior roles. So maybe companies aren't discovering that developers are useless. Maybe they're discovering that writing code is becoming cheaper, while engineering judgment is becoming more valuable. But that creates another problem. If AI takes away too much of the work juniors traditionally learned from... where do the next generation of senior engineers come from? Maybe AI isn't killing software engineering. Maybe it's changing what a software engineer is actually paid for. Developers: are we watching the end of software engineering as we knew it, or the beginning of a much better version of it?

posts.text: Building a product in 2027 may be the cheapest it has ever been. A few years ago, if you wanted to turn an idea into a working product, you needed access to engineers, time, and usually a decent amount of money. For many founders, the cost of building was the first major barrier between an idea and the market. That barrier is disappearing quickly. With vibe coding and increasingly capable agents, a small team can now build and ship things that would have required a much larger engineering team not too long ago. That changes the ecosystem. If someone can spend $20 and get an MVP into the hands of customers, having the ability to build is no longer much of a competitive advantage. And when everyone can build, I think we will start paying much more attention to what happens after the product is built. > Who understands the customer better? > Who can identify the right problem? > Who can make better product decisions? > Who can earn trust, distribute the product and turn feedback into something useful? The cost of creating software is falling. The cost of understanding people is going up. This is also why I’m thinking deeply about what happens to entry-level talent over the next 12 to 18 months. If a company can use AI to produce the first version of a product without hiring five junior developers, what exactly will create opportunities for those developers? I don’t think the answer is to panic and abandon technology. Quite the opposite. If you are early in your career, I would be very careful about becoming someone whose only value is “I can write code.” That skill is becoming easier to access. > Learn to understand the problem behind the code. > Learn how products work. Learn how customers behave. >Learn to debug, reason, communicate and make decisions. >Learn how to use AI without outsourcing your thinking to it. The same applies to people entering product, design, marketing, data and other parts of the workforce. I believe the next advantage will belong to people who can combine technical leverage with human judgment. We are entering a period where building will become cheaper, faster and more accessible. The interesting question is no longer, “Can you build it?” It is becoming, “Do you know what is worth building, why it matters, and what to do when the first version fails?” That is the conversation I want more young talent to start having now, before the market forces them to have it.

posts.author: Reece Sim
posts.headline: Building ThemeSpot - AI content management and theme development for HubSpot
posts.text: If your developer refuses to let you contribute with AI, or gate-keeps source code, it's time to let them go. As a web developer, I think it's so fucking cool that we can now invite our users to collaborate on features and code with us directly. Over the past two decades, web developers have gate-kept code.. Because it's too easy to break, too risky, they say. (and they want the recurring revenue) I always saw it as my job to make myself redundant after a project, especially on something simple like a website. Small updates and maintenance were like a thorn in my side rather than what I wanted to be doing every day, which was building features and digital experiences. AI made the code itself almost irrelevant, but it opened the door to new, and great product possibilities. If I design a harness correctly, by providing the right tools, infrastructure, and context, my users can write code with AI just as good as I can. That's incredible. It means good feedback just gets translated into code, and that you can build your own features, and customize your product experience to however you want to use it. Developers aren't out of a job, but code writers certainly are. True developers are euphoric right now, building more ambitious projects than ever before. I believe the future of all SaaS is pay to use a hosted version, pay for outcomes, work in a hackable UI, and you'll bring your own intelligence or pay a laziness tax on-platform. If your new app idea is selling tokens at a markup, you've already lost, you'd have higher margins selling outcomes. And if you're consuming tokens at a markup, hiring a developer will eventually be cheaper than all the rented software you pay for. A couple of things I've built recently where my clients can now collaborate directly: 1. A HubSpot developer project, with custom tools, hooks, and context files on how to maintain and improve the repo without me, how to debug deployment and a linter to ensure quality stays high. The client is free to vibe code whatever he wants into his website. 2. ThemeSpot - A HubSpot app that lets you vibe code entire themes, convert designs into pixel perfect HubSpot sites, manage content, QA websites, automate SEO and more. I can't wait to get to my terminal in the morning, all the mundane stuff is abstracted away. Pictured below: Non-technical C-suite asking for deploy logs, that's new!

posts.text: India's tech job market isn't "good" or "bad" right now. It's splitting in two. Naukri's September data shows: → Overall white-collar hiring: up 2% year on year → General software/IT hiring: down 4% → AI/ML hiring: up 20% In August, AI/ML hiring was up 31%, led by Hyderabad (+48%). The pattern is clear. Companies aren't hiring fewer people across the board. They're hiring for different skills. A few more signals from this week: → Global tech layoffs have crossed 1.63 lakh this year, and AI is cited in about 56% of them. → Oracle's latest round reportedly affects 1,000+ employees in India. → TCS planned only about 25,000 fresher offers for FY27, down from 44,000 last year. → GCCs (global capability centres) are still growing, with Hyderabad up 28% in August. What this means if you're a developer or fresher: Generic skills face more competition. Being "just another" full-stack or SDE profile is harder than it was. Pair your core stack (MERN, DevOps, Android, backend) with AI/LLM integration, cloud and security. Look beyond the big mass recruiters. GCCs, product companies and tier-2 cities like Coimbatore and Vadodara are showing stronger fresher growth. Watch the Q2 results: TCS (8 Oct), HCLTech (12 Oct), Infosys (23 Oct). Their headcount and fresher commentary will set the tone for the next quarter. My view: this is a skills shift, not a market collapse. The people who adapt will have the advantage. What's the one skill you're upskilling in this quarter? posts.headline: Principal Recruitment Consultant - Mobile & Testing | CTO/Tech Roundtable Host 🎤 · Visit my website
posts.text: My two cents on the current market: AI demand is accelerating quickly. Job ads requiring AI capability have roughly doubled over the past year, with AI skills now appearing across a significant proportion of software and data roles. AI Engineers are a clear example, with demand reportedly up around 150%. The supply of people with genuine hands-on AI experience simply isn’t keeping up. That shortage is creating a new tier of candidate. People who can genuinely build and implement AI are commanding strong packages, with some offers now including access to AI tooling and tokens. We’re also seeing experienced technical leaders getting back into the code. Even CTO-level candidates are exploring Software Engineering roles because they want to be hands-on with AI. At the same time, the broader tech market feels much quieter. The traditional domino effect of hiring has slowed down. When someone leaves, organisations are increasingly choosing to absorb the workload and “do more with less”. Job flow has slowed, salaries and contract rates have flattened, and junior and mid-level opportunities continue to decline as AI takes on tasks that previously helped develop less experienced engineers. However, specialist expertise remains highly valued. When businesses need niche technical knowledge or a specific capability delivered quickly, they’re still prepared to pay for it.

posts.text: Amazon loves: Heaps, Graph BFS, Intervals. Google loves: DP, Backtracking, Trees. Microsoft loves: Strings, Hashing, DP. You don't have to be ready for all 50 patterns. You have to be ready for the 10-15 your target company keeps asking. The DSA round is a pattern-targeting test, and the targets are fully public. Three moves separate the candidates who clear from the ones still applying. 1. Pick the shortlist first. Three companies, not thirty. Until you name the three, every problem you solve is a guess and every sheet you open is the wrong one. 2. Read 30 recent interview reports per company on LeetCode Discuss, GFG, and Glassdoor. Tag the pattern in each. By the 90th report, the top 5-8 patterns repeat so loudly you cannot miss them. 3. Drill those 5-8 until you can write the template blind, spot them in fresh problems under 90 seconds, and code the optimal under 25 minutes. Six weeks of focused work, not six months of random sheets. That's exactly what this DSA + System Design + AI Bootcamp is designed for—career outcomes, not just theory. If you’re a student, fresher, or someone looking to build real-world experience, this is an opportunity to learn, contribute, and work on real projects with a growing technology company. 🔎 Current Internship Opportunities 👥 HR & Recruitment Intern Help us with talent sourcing, candidate screening, interview coordination, recruitment operations, and HR processes. 💻 Frontend Developer Intern Work with React, JavaScript/TypeScript, responsive UI, APIs, Git, and modern web technologies. ⚙️ Backend Developer Intern Work with APIs, backend services, databases, authentication, integrations, and AI-powered applications. ☁️ Cloud / DevOps Intern Get hands-on exposure to cloud platforms, Linux, Docker, CI/CD, deployment, monitoring, and DevOps workflows. 📊 Product Manager Intern Work on product research, requirements, user stories, documentation, feature planning, and collaboration with engineering teams. 🗄️ Database Intern Work with SQL, PostgreSQL, database design, data management, queries, and backend database integration. 🌱 Who Can Apply? We welcome: • Students • Freshers • Recent graduates • Self-taught candidates • Candidates with academic or personal projects • People who are motivated to learn and build You don't need years of experience. We’re looking for curiosity, commitment, communication, and a willingness to learn. 💰 Internship Compensation These are unpaid internship positions. The internship is focused on providing: ✅ Real project experience ✅ Practical technical/business exposure ✅ Mentorship and guidance ✅ Team collaboration experience ✅ Internship certificate ✅ Portfolio/GitHub project experience ✅ Potential consideration for future paid or full-time opportunities based on performance 📍 Work Arrangement Remote / Hybrid 🕐 Internship Type Full-Time / Part-Time 📩 How to Apply Interested candidates can apply through LinkedIn with: 📄 Updated Resume 🔗 GitHub / Portfolio (for technical roles) 💼 LinkedIn Profile When applying, mention the position you are interested in. For example: “Frontend Developer Intern – Corivo Tech” We’re looking forward to meeting the next generation of builders, problem-solvers, and future professionals. 🚀 Join Corivo Tech. Learn. Build. posts.text: #hiring Senior Hydraulic Engineer Apply here: https://lnkd.in/ghDSh2Ax Project Overview: The Project is a greenfield mining, process, material handling and ship loading project with a focus on sustaining production, minimizing environmental impacts, strengthening long-term relationships with neighboring communities and fostering local economic development. Job Summary: In this role, you will conduct field investigations and plan specifications for hydrology & hydraulic design for large projects. You will lead flood analysis, special studies, and interpret regulations. You will participate in new business efforts, interview clients, develop estimates, and participate in proposal preparation. Your technical expertise will contribute to project flood risk prevention and mitigation. Major Responsibilities: Evaluate, select, and apply standard hydrology and hydraulic engineering methods, preparing flood analysis including hydrologic and hydraulic modeling, flood risk and impact assessments, flood protection and mitigation, river training and diversion, riverine erosion and scour protection design, stormwater management and drainage design, sediment control design, and associated permitting applications produced for the project for both permanent and temporary facilities as required.Provide oversight of value engineering, constructability reviews, safety reviews, and O&M reviews.Coordinate civil or structural engineering designs with hydrology and hydraulic assessments.Conduct review of hydrology and hydraulic interpretative reports and work with geotechnical consultants to produce high quality co coordinated submissions.Develop plans and schedules and coordinate each phase of hydrologic and hydraulics design development for motorways, local roads, and interchanges and grading.Oversee outside hydrology and hydraulic consultants hired by Bechtel or the client to perform these tasks.Provide input to reports and may provide technical assistance to other hydrology and hydraulic personnel.Assist project and construction management in identifying and complying with project requirements related to addressing issues as they arise during project execution.Ensure coordination of Hydrology and Hydraulic engineering work with civil and structural, geotechnical engineering, and other engineering disciplines to deliver well integrated, efficient and safe designs.Develop and review hydraulic and hydrological models using software, including TUFLOW.Mentor and support junior engineers and modeller, fostering technical development and continuous improvement within the team. Education and Experience Requirements: Bachelors degree
